newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany starts budget debate, tax row rumbles.
newsitem.headline: Germany starts budget debate, tax row rumbles.

text.p: Germany on Tuesday kicked off a four-day debate on Finance Minister Theo Waigel's 1997 budget, intended to ready state finances for European monetary union, but wrangling on tax plans continued behind the scenes.
Waigel was ill and absent from parliament, but the message from his parliamentary state secretary Irmgard Kawatzki was the one he has been repeating since unveiling his budget plans in July.
"This is a savings and consolidation budget," she told the Bundestag lower house. "With it the federal government has made its contribution towards fulfilling the Maastricht criteria."
The federal budget plans belt-tightening savings of 11 billion marks, with 1997 outlays totalling 440 billion marks ($290.7 billion).

The federal deficit is set at 53.3 billion marks, putting Germany on course for a total deficit of 2.5 percent of gross domestic product, and allowing a clear safety margin against the Maastricht treaty's three percent ceiling.
No major amendments are expected to the measure, which should be secured by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's 10-seat coalition majority in a final Bundestag vote on Friday.

In a lacklustre debate, government and opposition speakers rehearsed arguments played out in months of rows triggered by spending overshoots and drops in revenue estimates before the budget draft finally cleared parliament's committee stage.

Karl Diller of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) accused Waigel of "trickery" in drafting his finance package. He said that a borrowing overshoot of 13 billion marks this year would be repeated in 1997.
"This government is stumbling from one hole in the budget to the next," Diller said, adding that Germans have lost confidence that Kohl's government could ever create new jobs.

With German unemployment at a post-unification high of over four million, cuts in job programmes will hit ordinary Germans and undermine confidence in monetary union, said Christa Luft of the reformed communist Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS).

"People want to know their own fates -- the Maastricht criteria mean little to them," Luft said, adding of her east German support base "Imagine the fears of the people facing a second currency shock after the first one in 1990."
While the budget debate is likely to have little impact on the final outcome of Friday's vote, there was still a great deal more to play for over the 1997 tax bill.
The SPD has used its majority in the Bundesrat upper house of parliament to veto the abolition of wealth taxes. Parliamentary mediation talks have been deadlocked for weeks.
Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) had on Monday threatened to let the bill fail. But his CSU coalition partners said on Tuesday the measure could still be saved.

Michael Glos, head of Bavarian CSU deputies, told reporters after a meeting of leaders from Kohl's 14-year coalition that leaders of SPD-controlled states were showing more realism and the coalition still hoped for a compromise.
SPD parliament leader Rudolf Scharping also hinted at compromise, saying he would raise alternatives when the parliamentary budget debate continues on Wednesday.

The bill's failure, Glos warned, would mean big revenue losses for Germany's 16 states because the wealth tax would be automatically scrapped next year after being ruled illegal by the constitutional court.
But, he added, any possible damage to Germany's chance of qualifying for monetary union would be "repairable".
